screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of queue positions 1-12 after Batch 07 publication.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: The Impact of Localized Muscle Mass on Sprint Mechanics During the Swing and Stance Phases of Division I Collegiate American Football Players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This cross-sectional study assessed 108 Division I male football players grouped as Skills, Mids, and Bigs. Lower-extremity muscle volumes were measured with MRI and maximal-sprint stance and swing times with inertial sensors. Stepwise regressions found that the muscle-volume variables associated with shorter or longer phase times differed across position groups, supporting position-specific relationships rather than one generalized hypertrophy profile.
records.limitations: The associations are cross-sectional and cannot show that changing a specific muscle's size will change sprint mechanics. Testing occurred across multiple sites with possible procedural variation, stepwise models may overfit correlated muscle measures, and the work evaluated linear sprint phase times in one male collegiate program rather than change of direction, performance adaptation, or injury.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the findings to generate position-specific profiling questions, not to prescribe isolated hypertrophy or deliberately limit a muscle based on regression coefficients. Training transfer requires longitudinal validation.

records.sourceFile: Association between collision sport career duration and gait performance in male collegiate student-athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: A cross-sectional sample of 168 male collegiate football, lacrosse, ice hockey, and wrestling athletes completed instrumented single- and dual-task gait testing. Self-reported collision-sport career duration was not significantly associated with gait speed, stride length, cognitive accuracy, or dual-task costs, including single-task gait speed beta -0.004, P=.35 and dual-task gait speed beta -0.003, P=.57.
records.limitations: Career duration and continuity of collision exposure were self-reported, sport rule differences and actual head-impact dose were unavailable, and only healthy college-aged men were studied. The cross-sectional null findings from clinical gait tasks do not address later-life effects or exclude neurological changes detectable by other methods.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not interpret normal gait or a null group association as proof that repetitive head impacts are harmless. Use gait as one clinical measure and preserve longitudinal symptom, exposure, and multimodal assessment.

records.sourceFile: Feedback of GPS training data within professional English soccer A comparison of decision making and perceptions between coaches players and (1).pdf
records.evidenceSummary: An online survey of 176 professional-soccer coaches, performance staff, and players found that all stakeholder groups considered training data at least somewhat important for reflection and decisions. Coaches prioritized high-intensity actions and work-rate measures; players preferred total distance, high-speed running, and sprint feedback. Too much information, poor communication, and lack of a common goal were prominent barriers.
records.limitations: The convenience sample was recruited through social media and personal networks, was small relative to professional soccer, allowed clustered responses from the same environments, and measured perceptions rather than verified behavior or performance change. Findings concerned GPS data and should not be generalized to every monitoring method.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat feedback design as a communication and decision problem. More data are not automatically more useful; align the purpose, audience, metric set, delivery method, and intended action before distributing reports.

records.sourceFile: Hamstring injury occurrence in elite soccer players   after preseason strength training with eccentric overload.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Thirty elite male soccer players from two Swedish teams were randomized to ordinary training or 16 additional flywheel hamstring sessions over 10 preseason weeks. Across the 10-month observation period, hamstring injuries occurred in 3 of 15 trained players versus 10 of 15 controls, while the training group also improved isokinetic hamstring strength and maximal running speed.
records.limitations: The trial was small and unblinded, ordinary football exposure was not recorded in detail, injuries were registered by team personnel, and the control-group injury occurrence was unusually high. The intervention combined concentric and eccentric flywheel work, so the findings do not isolate a universal exercise, dose, or mechanism.
records.synthesisCaution: The study supports preseason eccentric-overload hamstring preparation but does not justify treating one device or protocol as sufficient prevention. Integrate progressive sprint exposure, strength, availability, and injury surveillance.

records.sourceFile: How does the workload applied during the training week and the contextual factors affect the physical responses of professional soccer players in the match.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: One season of GPS training and match records from two Spanish professional soccer teams was modeled with player and contextual effects. Conditional R-squared values were 0.51 for match total distance, 0.58 for high-intensity running distance, and 0.60 for sprint distance. Higher weekly training total distance was negatively associated with match output, while training high-intensity distance was positively associated; position, season period, division, and opposition quality also mattered.
records.limitations: This observational association cannot establish that reducing weekly volume or increasing high-intensity distance causes better match output. Results came from two teams, depended on the selected GPS thresholds and mixed-effects specification, and did not fully capture tactical, technical, wellness, or internal-load influences.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the model as local planning evidence, not a universal microcycle formula. Re-estimate relationships within the team and interpret weekly load alongside role, tactics, availability, match minutes, and recovery.

records.sourceFile: Cannabis use and sport - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review included 37 studies, mostly cross-sectional work in elite and university athletes. Across 11 prevalence studies involving 46,202 respondents, approximately 23.4% reported cannabis use in the prior 12 months. Two studies reported negative performance effects and two reported no effect; no eligible literature directly evaluated athletic recovery.
records.limitations: The evidence was primarily level-4, self-reported, cross-sectional, and heterogeneous in population, cannabis product, dose, timing, and outcome. THC and CBD effects were not interchangeable, recovery claims lacked direct evidence, and sport policies described in the 2020 review can change.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not present cannabis or CBD as a proven recovery tool or infer impairment from use history alone. Use confidential clinical screening, current policy verification, product-risk education, and individualized assessment.

records.sourceFile: Cardiovascular Health of Retired    Field-Based Athletes A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Thirteen studies included 4,350 retired male football and soccer athletes aged approximately 42 to 66 years; eight studies had controls. Findings were mixed: several studies reported elevated systolic blood pressure, all reporting LDL comparisons found higher LDL, and coronary calcium and carotid plaque were generally similar to controls. Retired linemen had about twice the cardiometabolic-syndrome prevalence of nonlinemen.
records.limitations: Risk-factor definitions and reporting were inconsistent, most evidence was observational and vulnerable to selection and survivor bias, and body mass and postcareer behavior confounded sport-history comparisons. Evidence covered men from only football and soccer and did not support a single pooled retired-athlete risk estimate.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not assume prior elite fitness protects cardiovascular health after retirement or that all former athletes share the same risk. Build transition and long-term screening around current body composition, blood pressure, lipids, activity, symptoms, and position history.

records.sourceFile: Clinical risk factors for Achilles   tendinopathy- a systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Ten cohort studies were retained from 5,111 records, and every included study had high risk of bias. Limited evidence implicated nine factors, including prior lower-limb tendinopathy or fracture, ofloxacin exposure, cold-weather training, lower plantar-flexor strength, selected gait features, moderate alcohol use, and renal or transplant-related factors. Twenty-six proposed factors, including overweight, static foot posture, and physical activity level, were not associated.
records.limitations: All included cohorts had high risk of bias, clinical populations and definitions were heterogeneous, English-only selection was used, and data could not be pooled. Several signals arose from medical populations such as heart-transplant recipients and may not transfer to athletes.
records.synthesisCaution: The review does not support a universal Achilles screening checklist or causal risk score. Use prior history, medication and medical context, symptoms, capacity, and exposure to guide individualized assessment while avoiding unsupported foot-posture or body-mass claims.

records.sourceFile: Core body temperatures in intermittent sports - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Thirty-four studies reported competition core temperatures in at least 386 adult intermittent-sport athletes. Four studies found no hyperthermia, 24 found modest hyperthermia with peak core temperature between 38.5 and 39.5 degrees Celsius, and six found marked hyperthermia at or above 39.5 degrees. Most studies were observational, and data were summarized descriptively rather than pooled.
records.limitations: Substantial heterogeneity in sports, competition duration, environmental conditions, athlete level, sampling schedules, and temperature methods prevented meta-analysis. The descriptive peak categories do not establish an individual heat-illness threshold or prove which cooling or acclimation intervention works best in intermittent sport.
records.synthesisCaution: Plan for meaningful heat strain but do not use a single core-temperature value in isolation. Combine environment, acclimatization, symptoms, medical risk, hydration opportunity, workload, and emergency procedures.

records.sourceFile: Current Evidence for the Use of Jugular Vein Compression Collars in Sport - A Systematic Review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review included 15 jugular-vein-compression-collar studies. Collar groups showed favorable signals in selected white-matter, short-term neurocognitive, vascular, and pulse-pressure outcomes, but concussion incidence did not differ significantly. The evidence was concentrated in adolescents and preliminary sport or tactical cohorts rather than long-term clinical outcomes.
records.limitations: Most studies randomized by team rather than individual, collar use was visible, off-season head impacts were not controlled, and the evidence was dominated by adolescent samples. The Q-Collar inventor advised the company that funded most included studies, creating an important conflict-of-interest concern despite the review's low risk-of-bias rating.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not describe jugular compression collars as proven concussion prevention. Favor established exposure reduction, technique, recognition, removal, and clinical care while treating imaging or short-term surrogate findings as preliminary.

records.sourceFile: Dehydration Impairs Cognitive Performance- A Meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Thirty-three studies contributed 280 effect estimates from 413 participants dehydrated by 1% to 6% body mass. Overall cognitive impairment was small, effect size -0.21, with larger effects for attention, -0.52, motor coordination, -0.40, and executive function, -0.24. Effects were larger above 2% body-mass loss, -0.28, than at or below 2%, -0.14.
records.limitations: Protocols, dehydration methods, cognitive tasks, accuracy and reaction-time outcomes, and participant characteristics varied, with significant heterogeneity. Mood, thirst, mental exertion, heat, and exercise could contribute to effects, samples were often convenient and small, and the 2% comparison is a subgroup pattern rather than a precise individual threshold.
records.synthesisCaution: Prevent avoidable dehydration, especially before decision-heavy work, but do not treat 2% body-mass loss as a universal cliff. Interpret body-mass change with environment, task, baseline hydration, symptoms, and individual response.

records.sourceFile: Do multi-ingredient protein supplements augment resistance training-induced gains in skeletal muscle mass and strength - A systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 trials.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Thirty-five resistance-training trials involving 1,387 participants compared multi-ingredient protein supplements with placebo or other supplements. Versus all non-multi-ingredient conditions, pooled gains favored multi-ingredient products for fat-free mass by 0.80 kg, lower-body one-repetition maximum by 4.22 kg, and upper-body one-repetition maximum by 2.56 kg. Direct comparisons showed no superiority over protein-only supplementation.
records.limitations: Only retrievable English-language trials were included, ingredient combinations and comparators varied, and moderate heterogeneity remained. Pooled advantage over all controls combines placebo and active comparisons, while the protein-only comparison indicates that extra ingredients may not explain the apparent benefit.
records.synthesisCaution: Prioritize adequate total protein, diet, and progressive resistance training before adding multi-ingredient products. Do not infer that a branded blend is superior to protein alone, and verify safety, dose, cost, and third-party testing.
